Figure 2. Predicted docking poses and pocket environments of Gpr2 WT. (a, b) ascr#3; (c, d) ascr#18. Each pair shows a 3D pocket view and the corresponding Maestro 2D interaction diagram [6] for the lowest-scoring pose. In the 3D views, the receptor is shown as a purple cartoon, pocket residues as yellow sticks, and ascr#3 and ascr#18 in cyan and magenta, respectively. Original residue numbering is retained.

Figure 4. Predicted docking poses and pocket environments of Gpr2 N84V. (a, b) ascr#3; (c, d) ascr#18. Each pair shows a 3D pocket view and the corresponding Maestro 2D interaction diagram for the lowest-scoring pose. Colors follow Figure 2, and residue numbering matches WT.

Figure 5. Predicted docking poses and pocket environments of Gpr2 V368R. (a, b) ascr#3; (c, d) ascr#18. Each pair shows a 3D pocket view and the corresponding Maestro 2D interaction diagram for the lowest-scoring pose. Colors follow Figure 2, and residue numbering matches WT.

Figure 1. Ligand heavy-atom RMSD under three structural alignment schemes. Trajectories were aligned using the whole receptor, the transmembrane helical core, or the local pocket backbone, with each trajectory referenced to its own initial production structure. Curves show a 1 ns centered moving average of data sampled every 100 ps. Shading marks the 50–100 ns comparison window. Each system is represented by one 100 ns trajectory.

Figure 2. Arg189–carboxylate interactions in the Gpr2 N84V–ascr#18 complex. (a) Simulation snapshot at 64.64 ns. The receptor is shown as purple ribbons; ascr#18 and Arg189 are shown as sticks with magenta and yellow carbon atoms, respectively. The dashed line indicates an Arg189–carboxylate hydrogen bond with a donor–acceptor distance of 2.77 Å. (b) Occupancy of at least one Arg189–carboxylate hydrogen bond during 50–100 ns: 93.6% for N84V–ascr#18 and 0% for WT–ascr#18 and N84V–ascr#3. Frames were sampled every 100 ps, using the hydrogen-bond criteria defined in the text.

Figure 3. Changes in ligand anchoring in V368R–ascr#3 simulations initiated from two alternative poses. (a,b) Time-dependent salt-bridge occupancies for the Arg368-directed (a) and Arg189-directed (b) starting poses. Each panel compares the designed Arg368–carboxylate or Arg189–carboxylate contact with the Arg345–carboxylate contact. Shading marks the 50–100 ns comparison window. (c) Arg345–carboxylate contact occupancies during 50–100 ns in the two additional trajectories and the WT–ascr#3, V368R–ascr#18, and original V368R–ascr#3 trajectories. Bars indicate salt-bridge occupancy using a distance cutoff of ≤4 Å; diamonds indicate the occupancy of short, near-linear hydrogen bonds. Each starting pose was simulated for 100 ns.

Figure 3-1. Sequential calibration workflow for the ODE and dual-channel models.
The upper panel shows mixed-sample design, ODE calibration, and dual-channel regression. The lower panel shows the intended workflow for estimating Mi density from paired smartphone readings. Prescribed pigment targets are used to calibrate the ODE, while regression uses color features calculated from the actual ODE outputs. Generated with OpenAI GPT Image 2.

Figure 3-2. ODE pigment calibration at different background densities.
Panels A and B show P3 and P18, respectively. Colors distinguish Ce background densities. Dashed lines with crosses indicate prescribed pigment targets, solid lines with circles indicate simulated 8 h total pigment concentrations, and gray dotted lines indicate the blank.

Figure 3-3. Net pigment accumulation in representative mixed samples.
Panels A and B show simulated time courses for blank, Mi-only, Ce-only, and mixed samples in P3 and P18. Net pigment is calculated by subtracting the matched channel blank at each time point.

Figure 3-4. Distribution of mixed samples in dual-channel color space.
The horizontal and vertical axes show the simulated P3 and P18 smartphone color indices. Point color indicates Mi density. Solid lines connect samples with fixed Mi density, while dashed lines connect samples with fixed Ce density. Arrows indicate the directions of increasing Mi or Ce density.

Figure 3-5. Mi Density predictions and comparison of single- and dual-channel models.
Panel A compares known and predicted Mi densities for the dual-channel model; the dashed line indicates ideal agreement. Panel B compares the RMSEs of P3-only, P18-only, and dual-channel models on the same simulated evaluation set.
